paragraphs: Optimizing a system governed by partial differential equations can require repeatedly solving those equations as design parameters change. This makes tasks such as inferring physical properties or designing structures expensive. The paper proposes Amortized Finite Element Analysis, or AmorFEA, which trains a neural network to supply accurate solutions for use during optimization.

The network learns by minimizing the physical potential energy underlying the equations and their finite element formulation. Consequently, training does not require a collection of example solutions generated by costly conventional solvers. The finite element basis still defines the family of possible solutions, connecting the method to the variational structure of traditional finite element analysis.

The central benefit is to spread the work of learning to solve these equations across subsequent optimization steps. The abstract reports faster PDE-constrained optimization than a traditional workflow combining finite element analysis with the adjoint method. Its contribution is therefore both a solver substitute and a training approach that preserves many finite element advantages while avoiding repeated conventional solves.
icml-2020-amortized-finite-element-analy.tldr: AmorFEA learns PDE solutions directly from physical energy objectives to accelerate optimization that would otherwise require repeated finite element solves.

paragraphs: Training examples can differ in how much they help a particular prediction task. This paper introduces Data Valuation using Reinforcement Learning, or DVRL, to estimate that usefulness while also training the predictor. The intended applications include understanding datasets, adapting between domains, identifying corrupted examples, and learning robustly from imperfect data.

A data value estimator learns the probability that each example will be used to train the predictor. Its feedback comes from a reinforcement signal reflecting performance on the target task. This ties the assigned values to what helps the prediction problem, and allows the estimator and predictor to develop together rather than treating valuation as a separate fixed preprocessing step.

Across the reported datasets and application settings, DVRL produces better value estimates than the compared alternatives. Corrupted-sample discovery is close to the reference of knowing the noisy samples in advance in many regimes. The abstract also reports improvements of 14.6% for domain adaptation and 10.8% for robust learning over the stated state-of-the-art comparisons.
icml-2020-data-valuation-using-reinforce.tldr: DVRL learns which training examples are useful through task-performance feedback, improving data valuation and several learning applications in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Some data naturally arrives as a set, where changing the order of its elements should not change its probabilistic interpretation. Point clouds are one example. The paper addresses modeling such exchangeable data, focusing on existing approaches that either constrain the number of elements or offer limited distributions over data that has not been observed.

Energy-Based Processes extend energy-based modeling to this setting. A neural network parameterizes the energy function, giving the model a flexible way to describe distributions over sets. The proposed construction permits sets without imposing a fixed cardinality restriction. These two properties address distinct needs: flexibility in what a set may contain and flexibility in how many elements it may have.

The authors also develop an efficient procedure for training these models. They report state-of-the-art performance on tasks including point cloud generation, classification, denoising, and image completion. The range of applications demonstrates the proposed framework in both generating data and reasoning about incomplete or corrupted observations, alongside its broader contribution to modeling exchangeable sets.
icml-2020-energy-based-processes-for-exc.tldr: Energy-Based Processes model flexible distributions over exchangeable sets without restricting set size, with strong reported results across several tasks.

paragraphs: Feature selection asks which inputs a predictive model actually needs. Although this problem has been widely studied for linear models, the paper focuses on selecting inputs while learning nonlinear functions with neural networks. Its goal is to train an effective regression or classification model while retaining only a small subset of the available features.

The method penalizes the number of selected features, expressed through the zero norm. Because discrete selection is difficult to optimize directly with gradient descent, the authors use a continuous relaxation of Bernoulli variables. These relaxed stochastic gates allow the selection parameters to be learned alongside the predictive function, bringing the choice of inputs into the same optimization process as prediction.

The paper provides an information-theoretic argument for using Bernoulli distributions in feature selection. Experiments on synthetic and real data report improvements over commonly used methods in both predictive performance and feature selection. These findings support the value of learning sparsity together with nonlinear relationships, rather than judging input usefulness only through a linear estimation setting.
icml-2020-feature-selection-using-stocha.tldr: Stochastic gates make feature-count regularization trainable with gradient descent, jointly selecting inputs and learning nonlinear predictors.

paragraphs: Large neural networks can contain much smaller subnetworks that retain strong predictive performance. This paper investigates whether such subnetworks can be shown to exist and found efficiently. Its pruning method starts with an empty network and repeatedly adds important neurons from a larger network, building the compact model through greedy forward selection.

The theoretical result depends on starting from a sufficiently large pretrained network. Under that condition, the selection strategy is guaranteed to find small subnetworks with lower loss than networks trained directly using gradient descent. The authors also extend their results to pruning networks with random weights. These statements give theoretical support to a process often approached through empirical pruning rules.

Experiments improve prior pruning results for compact ImageNet architectures, including ResNet, MobileNetV2/V3, and ProxylessNet. The theory and MobileNet experiments also support fine-tuning the selected subnetwork so that it retains information from the larger model. This recommendation concerns how to use the extracted network, alongside the paper’s contribution to how that network is selected.
icml-2020-good-subnetworks-provably-exis.tldr: Greedily adding neurons yields compact subnetworks with conditional theoretical guarantees and improved reported pruning results.

paragraphs: Repairing a program from compiler feedback requires connecting an error message to the relevant symbols and locations in source code. Training such systems is also difficult because labeled repair examples are relatively scarce. This paper tackles both issues in DrRepair, a system that combines graph-based reasoning with self-supervised pretraining.

Its program-feedback graph links symbols in the source code with symbols in diagnostic feedback. A graph neural network then models the reasoning needed for repair through these connections. To expand training data, the authors use unlabeled programs available online to create additional repair examples. Those examples support pretraining before evaluation on the target repair applications.

The system is tested on introductory programming assignments in DeepFix and on program-synthesis outputs in SPoC. It achieves a 68.2% full repair rate on DeepFix and a 48.4% synthesis success rate on SPoC, substantially exceeding prior work as reported in the abstract. These results support addressing both the representation of diagnostic relationships and the shortage of repair training data.
icml-2020-graph-based-self-supervised-pr.tldr: DrRepair combines graphs linking code to diagnostic feedback with self-supervised pretraining to improve program repair and synthesis success.

paragraphs: Molecular generators must produce complex structures, which often makes them heavily parameterized and demanding of training data. This paper proposes a self-training approach that creates additional molecular targets during learning. The central idea is to use a model’s generated candidates, together with a property predictor, to expand the material from which the generator learns.

The authors first pretrain the generator and a simple property predictor. The predictor then supplies a likelihood model for filtering proposed structures. Stochastic expectation-maximization iterations generate additional targets and optimize the log-likelihood of candidate acceptance. The abstract explains that a simple rejection or reweighting sampler is sufficient because pretraining has already made the generator reasonably effective.

The reported experiments show significant gains over strong comparisons for both unconditional and conditional molecular design. For conditional design, the abstract reports an absolute improvement exceeding 10% over the previous state of the art. Results in program synthesis further demonstrate usefulness beyond molecules, supporting the broader idea of iteratively augmenting structured-generation targets through a learned acceptance model.
icml-2020-improving-molecular-design-by-.tldr: Iteratively filtering generated structures with a property predictor creates additional training targets and improves reported molecular-design performance.

paragraphs: Ordinary differential equations offer a way to interpret neural-network architectures, but their connection to convolutional networks without residual connections has been less clear. This paper introduces a differential-equation model with damping. Adjusting an interpolation coefficient allows the model to recover both a residual network and a non-residual convolutional network.

This construction places the two architectures within a common mathematical framework. The authors use Lyapunov analysis to establish better stability for the proposed model and connect that stability to improved robustness in the learned networks. Damping therefore plays two roles: it helps bridge the architectural interpretations and motivates a design intended to behave better under input disturbances.

On several image-classification benchmarks, the resulting approach substantially improves ResNet and ResNeXt accuracy when inputs contain stochastic noise or adversarial perturbations. An analysis of the loss landscape also shows improved robustness along the attack direction. Together, the reported evidence links the continuous-system interpretation to measured behavior under perturbed inputs, rather than leaving it solely as an architectural analogy.
icml-2020-interpolation-between-residual.tldr: A damped differential-equation model connects residual and non-residual networks and improves reported robustness to noisy and adversarial inputs.

paragraphs: When neural networks are applied to computationally difficult problems, attention often centers on what the model can learn. This paper examines an earlier obstacle: producing representative training examples. A model may appear successful on an NP-hard task if the procedure that generates its data actually concentrates on an easier part of that task.

Assuming NP is not equal to coNP, the authors prove that any polynomial-time sample generator for an NP-hard problem samples from an easier subproblem. The assumption is central to the stated theorem. The result shifts the discussion toward the computational difficulty of supplying training data, rather than treating data generation as a straightforward prerequisite to learning.

The empirical case study examines Conjunctive Query Containment. Common generation techniques produce biased datasets that lead practitioners to overestimate model accuracy. The authors consequently suggest that methods requiring dense, uniform samples from the target distribution cannot solve computationally hard problems through that route, because generating sufficiently large unbiased datasets is itself an obstacle.
icml-2020-its-not-what-machines-can-lear.tldr: Under NP ≠ coNP, efficient sample generation for NP-hard problems targets easier subproblems, exposing a potential source of misleading learning results.

paragraphs: Joint image filtering often combines input pixels through weighted averaging. The choice of weights determines how information is aggregated, but hand-designed weights can struggle with complex inputs. This paper proposes learning those weights with neural networks while addressing the computational difficulty of directly predicting the full, very large weight matrix.

The first component estimates aggregation weights from correlations between learned deep features. This supplies a low-rank representation of the matrix, but relies on inner products and therefore restricts what the weights can express. The second component learns a nonlinear function that predicts sparse residual corrections to the correlation matrix. Both components are learned together.

The resulting design combines a compact low-rank component with a sparse component that adds corrections beyond feature similarity alone. This makes learning the aggregation process more tractable while addressing a limitation of the initial approximation. Across a broad collection of joint-filtering tasks, the experiments report favorable comparisons with state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the usefulness of learning both components simultaneously.
icml-2020-learning-factorized-weight-mat.tldr: The method learns joint-filtering weights through low-rank deep-feature correlations plus sparse nonlinear corrections.

paragraphs: MetaFun addresses supervised meta-learning with an encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder turns labeled examples into a representation that the decoder uses to predict labels for new inputs. Its distinctive choice is to represent the labeled data as a function in an infinite-dimensional space, rather than compressing it into a finite-dimensional representation.

The method also changes how this representation is constructed. A learned neural update rule repeatedly improves the function, in a process resembling gradient descent over functions. The final function conditions the decoder’s predictions on unlabeled data. This makes iterative refinement part of the learned encoding procedure, rather than asking the encoder to produce its final representation in a single step.

The abstract reports state-of-the-art results on the large-scale few-shot classification benchmarks miniImageNet and tieredImageNet. It presents these results as evidence that encoder-decoder meta-learning approaches, including the style associated with conditional neural processes, can succeed in this setting. The contribution combines a different representation space with learned updates that adapt that representation to the available labeled examples.
icml-2020-metafun-meta-learning-with-ite.tldr: MetaFun iteratively updates a functional representation of labeled examples and reports state-of-the-art few-shot classification performance.

paragraphs: Multi-agent learning often trains agents together but requires them to act separately afterward. Decomposing a centralized value function for that purpose can impose restrictive structural assumptions. This paper proposes multi-agent determinantal Q-learning, built around Q-DPP, an extension of determinantal point processes to the multi-agent setting.

Q-DPP encourages agents to learn diverse behavioral models. According to the paper, this supports a natural factorization of joint Q-functions without prescribing structural constraints on the value function or requiring special network architectures. The framework also generalizes VDN, QMIX, and QTRAN on decentralizable cooperative tasks, connecting the proposed formulation to several established ways of coordinating agents.

To make sampling practical, the authors develop a linear-time sampler with a theoretical approximation guarantee. The sampling procedure also supports exploration by coordinating agents toward orthogonal directions in the state space during training. Evaluations on multiple cooperative benchmarks demonstrate effectiveness against state-of-the-art comparisons. The method therefore connects behavioral diversity to both value decomposition and coordinated exploration within centralized training.
icml-2020-multi-agent-determinantal-q-le.tldr: Q-DPP uses diverse agent behaviors to support joint-value factorization and coordinated exploration without prescribed value-function structure.

paragraphs: Top-k classification evaluates whether the correct class appears among a model’s k leading choices, making it useful when labels are ambiguous. Models are often trained using a surrogate loss rather than this error directly. The paper studies when optimizing such a surrogate is theoretically consistent with achieving optimal top-k classification.

The authors introduce a top-k preserving property to characterize Bayes-optimal predictions and resolve a non-uniqueness gap in previous analysis. They then define top-k calibration and prove that it is both necessary and sufficient for consistency. This provides a criterion for determining whether a surrogate loss aligns with the classification objective it is meant to support.

Using that criterion, the paper develops a broad family of calibrated surrogates based on Bregman divergences. It also shows that previously proposed hinge-like top-k losses are inconsistent. Of two newly proposed hinge-like losses, one is consistent and the other is not. Experiments illustrate the theoretical distinctions, showing why superficially similar training losses can have different consistency properties.
icml-2020-on-the-consistency-of-top-k-su.tldr: The paper characterizes top-k consistency through calibration and uses it to distinguish valid surrogate losses from inconsistent alternatives.

paragraphs: Robot control can involve conflicting objectives, so a single policy may not suit every preference among them. The paper seeks a dense, high-quality collection of policies representing different trade-offs. It focuses on continuous control, where actions vary continuously and multi-objective reinforcement learning had received comparatively limited attention.

The proposed evolutionary learning algorithm extends an existing reinforcement-learning method and adds a prediction model that guides learning. Its target is an approximation of the Pareto set: policies representing optimal trade-offs among objectives. Beyond discovering individual policies, the authors use Pareto analysis and interpolation to construct a continuous set of Pareto-optimal solutions, expanding the range of available preferences.

The work also introduces seven environments with continuous action spaces for evaluating multi-objective robot control. Experiments compare previous methods on these benchmark problems and show that the proposed approach finds a much denser, higher-quality set of Pareto policies. The reported benefit concerns the breadth and quality of the policy collection, allowing the learning process to serve multiple objective preferences.
icml-2020-prediction-guided-multi-object.tldr: Prediction-guided evolutionary reinforcement learning finds richer policy trade-offs for continuous robot control on seven proposed benchmark environments.

paragraphs: Extreme multi-label text classification assigns relevant labels to a text from a very large collection of possibilities. A useful system must represent the text effectively while handling the computational burden of that label collection. This paper introduces APLC-XLNet, combining a pretrained language model with a method for organizing labels during training.

The approach fine-tunes XLNet to produce a dense representation of the input text. Adaptive Probabilistic Label Clusters then approximate the cross-entropy loss by exploiting the imbalance in label frequencies. Forming these clusters explicitly reduces computation time. The method therefore addresses both the representation of the document and the expense of learning predictions across an extremely large label space.

Experiments cover five benchmark datasets, with new state-of-the-art results reported on four of them. These findings support combining pretrained text representations with a loss approximation designed around uneven label distributions. The contribution is a specific integration of language-model fine-tuning and efficient label handling, evaluated in the setting where texts may need multiple labels drawn from a very large vocabulary.
icml-2020-pretrained-generalized-autoreg.tldr: APLC-XLNet combines XLNet fine-tuning with probabilistic label clusters to reduce computation and improve extreme multi-label text classification.

paragraphs: In cooperative multi-agent tasks, agents may receive a shared reward while observing only their own parts of the situation. Learning good coordination then requires assigning credit: determining how the team’s outcome should guide each agent. This paper addresses that problem within centralized training followed by decentralized execution.

Q-value Path Decomposition, or QPD, separates the system’s global Q-values into individual agents’ Q-values. It uses integrated gradient attribution along trajectory paths to allocate credit. Earlier approaches restrict the representational relationship between the individual values and the global value. QPD instead performs the decomposition directly through attribution, giving the learning process another way to connect shared outcomes with individual policies.

The authors evaluate QPD on StarCraft II micromanagement tasks involving both homogeneous and heterogeneous teams. They report state-of-the-art performance against existing cooperative multi-agent reinforcement-learning algorithms in both settings. These results support trajectory-based value attribution as an effective mechanism for credit assignment when agents must coordinate from private observations but learn from a common measure of team success.
icml-2020-q-value-path-decomposition-for.tldr: QPD attributes global Q-values to individual agents along trajectory paths, improving reported cooperative performance on StarCraft II tasks.

paragraphs: Randomized smoothing certifies robustness by studying predictions under random input perturbations. Extending it to different measures of perturbation size has often required separate derivations. This paper proposes a general framework for choosing smoothing distributions and analyzing their guarantees, with both constructive results and limits on what current techniques can certify.

For an appropriate definition of optimality and a class of suitably well-behaved norms, the authors identify optimal distributions whose equal-density surfaces follow the norm’s Wulff crystal. They also introduce two complementary methods for deriving certified radii for any smoothing distribution. Combining these results substantially improves reported certified accuracy against perturbations measured by the l1 norm on standard datasets.

The limits use Banach-space cotype theory. When certification relies only on label statistics from randomly perturbed inputs, the authors rule out nontrivial certified accuracy against lp perturbations at the stated scale Ω(min(1, d^(1/p − 1/2))) in high dimension d. This qualification matters: the impossibility result concerns that information setting, while the constructive results explain how distribution geometry can improve achievable certificates.
icml-2020-randomized-smoothing-of-all-sh.tldr: A general theory of randomized smoothing improves l1 robustness certificates and establishes high-dimensional limits for methods using only perturbed-label statistics.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes difficult when an agent must explore a large collection of state-action pairs. Feature representations offer a way to reduce that complexity, but the paper notes that existing methods can lack guarantees or have regret growing exponentially with the planning horizon. MatrixRL addresses exploration through a compact representation of the transition model.

The algorithm adapts ideas from linear bandits to learn that representation while balancing exploration with the use of already acquired knowledge. Its reported regret bound is O(H² d log(T) √T), where H is the planning horizon and d is the number of features. The bound is independent of the number of state-action pairs and has polynomial dependence on H.

The paper also provides an equivalent kernelized algorithm that operates in a kernel Hilbert space without explicit features. Its bound replaces d with the kernel space’s effective dimension. These results identify representation dimension as the relevant complexity measure in the stated guarantees, showing how feature-based and kernel-based transition modeling can support theoretically controlled online exploration.
icml-2020-reinforcement-learning-in-feat.tldr: MatrixRL learns transition dynamics in feature or kernel space with regret bounds that depend on representation dimension rather than state-action count.

paragraphs: The classical bias-variance account suggests that increasing model complexity reduces bias but raises variance, producing a U-shaped risk curve. Neural networks often behave differently, with larger models generalizing better. This paper measures the two components separately to investigate how changes in network size can produce that apparently conflicting behavior.

Across the architectures, losses, and datasets considered, bias decreases with width while variance first rises and then falls. The authors find this bell-shaped variance pattern consistently in their experiments. Adding the measured bias and variance curves can produce several risk shapes depending on their relative sizes, with double descent appearing as one possibility. A theoretical analysis of two-layer linear networks with random first layers corroborates the findings.

The study also examines distribution shift and depth. On the evaluated out-of-distribution data, most accuracy loss is associated with increased bias, while variance rises less. Greater depth reduces bias and increases variance for both in-distribution and out-of-distribution data. These observations distinguish the measured effects of width, depth, and distribution shift within the same explanatory framework.
icml-2020-rethinking-bias-variance-trade.tldr: Measured neural-network variance rises and then falls with width, helping explain double descent and other observed generalization curves.

paragraphs: Selecting which examples to learn from is a common response to noisy labels. The difficult part is controlling selection so that a deep network benefits from its memorization behavior during training. This paper treats that control problem as something to learn automatically, drawing on ideas from automated machine learning.

The authors formulate the selection problem as function approximation and build a specialized search space around general patterns of the memorization effect. They then introduce a Newton algorithm to solve the resulting bilevel optimization efficiently. This couples the search for a useful selection function with the learning process that the function is intended to improve, rather than leaving selection control entirely to manual design.

The theoretical analysis guarantees a good approximation to critical points of the optimization problem. Experiments on benchmark and real-world datasets report substantially better results than state-of-the-art noisy-label approaches, together with greater efficiency than existing AutoML algorithms. The contribution combines a search space informed by training behavior with an optimization method designed to make searching that space practical.
icml-2020-searching-to-exploit-memorizat.tldr: The method automatically searches for sample-selection functions that exploit memorization patterns, improving reported noisy-label learning and search efficiency.

paragraphs: An inf-projection objective is defined by minimizing a joint function over an additional variable. The outer optimization then works with the value left after that minimization. This paper studies such objectives when they are non-convex and potentially non-smooth, covering difference-of-convex functions and a family of bi-convex functions as special cases.

The authors develop stochastic algorithms and establish first-order convergence toward a nearly stationary solution. The guarantees depend on different conditions imposed on the component functions. A nearly stationary point is the stated target, so the results do not amount to a general global-minimum guarantee. The framework enables efficient stochastic optimization for covered non-decomposable difference-of-convex and bi-convex problems.

Variance-based regularization provides the application used to demonstrate the approach. Experiments compare the inf-projection formulation and its stochastic algorithm with earlier stochastic methods that use a min-max formulation for the same effect. The reported effectiveness shows why changing the mathematical formulation can be useful: it brings the application within a class for which the paper develops both algorithms and convergence analysis.
icml-2020-stochastic-optimization-for-no.tldr: The paper develops stochastic methods with conditional convergence guarantees for non-convex inf-projection objectives and applies them to variance-based regularization.

paragraphs: Models trained to predict spatial and temporal dynamics may learn different useful perspectives from different data sources. This paper studies how to transfer knowledge from a collection of unsupervised predictive models into another predictive network. Its motivation includes helping target tasks that already have sufficient training examples, rather than treating transfer only as a remedy for scarce data.

The proposed differentiable framework, called transferable memory, draws knowledge from a bank of memory states belonging to multiple pretrained recurrent neural networks. A new recurrent structure, the Transferable Memory Unit, adaptively distills that knowledge and applies it to the target network. This makes the stored dynamics of several source models available within the target’s recurrent prediction process.

Across three spatiotemporal prediction benchmarks, the approach yields significant improvements over fine-tuning. The authors also report benefits from source pretext tasks that are less relevant to the target task. These findings support the idea that complementary knowledge from multiple predictive models can improve a new task, with adaptive transfer helping use information beyond the most obviously related source.
icml-2020-unsupervised-transfer-learning.tldr: Transferable memory adaptively distills multiple pretrained recurrent models into a target predictor, outperforming fine-tuning on three spatiotemporal benchmarks.

paragraphs: Quantization turns continuous latent representations into forms that can be stored compactly. This paper introduces a quantization algorithm for trained probabilistic models, including variational autoencoders. It separates quantization from model design and training, allowing a single trained model to support different trade-offs between compressed size and reconstruction distortion.

The algorithm adapts quantization accuracy using estimates of posterior uncertainty. The authors interpret it as an extension of arithmetic coding to the continuous domain. Its practical appeal is plug-and-play compression: the quantization stage can be adjusted after training instead of requiring the model to be trained around one fixed quantization scheme. The proposed approach supports both data and model compression.

Experiments demonstrate the importance of accounting for posterior uncertainty when choosing quantization precision. With a single standard variational autoencoder, the image-compression results outperform JPEG across a wide range of bit rates. Additional experiments on Bayesian neural word embeddings demonstrate applicability beyond image compression, supporting the method’s intended role as a reusable quantization procedure for probabilistic representations.
icml-2020-variational-bayesian-quantizat.tldr: Uncertainty-aware quantization enables adjustable compression of already-trained probabilistic models without tying training to a fixed quantization scheme.

paragraphs: A logical label records whether a label applies, whereas a label distribution expresses how strongly each label describes an example. Those degrees can represent ambiguity more precisely, but they are difficult to obtain directly. This paper proposes recovering such richer supervision from training datasets that contain only simpler logical labels.

The method treats each unknown label distribution as a latent vector and infers it through variational inference. It then uses multi-output regression to learn a predictive model from the resulting distribution-valued data. This creates a two-stage connection between the available annotations and the desired predictions: first infer degrees of relevance, then learn to predict those degrees from examples.

The authors evaluate distribution recovery on thirteen real-world label-distribution-learning datasets and predictive performance on ten multi-label datasets. Both sets of experiments support an advantage over the compared state-of-the-art approaches. The results matter because they assess both parts of the proposal: whether richer labels can be recovered and whether learning from the enhanced labels helps with prediction.
icml-2020-variational-label-enhancement-.tldr: Variational Label Enhancement infers graded label relevance from logical labels and uses the recovered distributions to train a predictor.

paragraphs: A video can have multiple plausible futures, differing in both content and motion. This makes prediction more demanding than identifying a single continuation. The paper proposes guiding predictions with analogous sequences retrieved from a training pool, called expert examples, to approximate the distribution of possible future developments.

The retrieved examples are used to construct a distribution from which plausible predictions can be sampled. A new optimization scheme incorporated into training supports efficient sampling. The framework can also be integrated with existing stochastic prediction models, making example guidance a component that can improve a predictor rather than requiring it to replace the entire prediction approach.

The reported experiments find significant improvements in quantitative evaluations and qualitative results when using this guidance. The authors also demonstrate prediction of motion from an unseen class without corresponding training data for that class. This supports the proposed use of analogous examples to guide multiple plausible futures, including the demonstrated case where the target motion class was absent during training.
icml-2020-video-prediction-via-example-g.tldr: Retrieved example sequences guide a distribution of plausible video futures, improving stochastic prediction and demonstrating transfer to an unseen motion class.
